title: Joy in the morning (Psalm 30)
hookLine: weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning

lines: WORRIES GROW TEETH IN THE DARK.
cards: Three in the morning, wide awake. Lying there with a fever, or sitting in a waiting room as the clock crawls past three. The night after a breakup, or bad news, or a fight you can't take back.

Things weigh more in the dark. Worries grow teeth. And then, sometimes without anything at all being fixed, the window goes gray, then pale, a bird starts up outside, and the same problem looks different in daylight.
Not solved. Just survivable. Psalm thirty puts that whole stretch of night into a single line.

teach.h: WEEPING STAYS THE NIGHT, LIKE A GUEST.
teach.b: Psalm thirty, in the King James Bible: "For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." The Hebrew picture is even more vivid.
The word for endure, yalin, means to lodge, to spend the night. Weeping comes in like an overnight guest. It's allowed in.
It stays the night. But it doesn't move in. In the morning, joy arrives, and the guest leaves.
The psalm is a thank-you, and it tells a story.

teach.h: I SAID, I SHALL NEVER BE MOVED.
teach.b: When things were going well, the writer got comfortable: "In my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved." Then God hid his face, he says, and he was troubled.
He fell ill, or nearly died; he talks about going down to the pit. He cried out, and he was healed.
Then the line about dancing: "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness." Sackcloth was the rough cloth people wore in grief.
God, the psalm says, took it off him, like a parent changing a child's clothes, and dressed him in joy.
The heading calls it a song at the dedication of the house, which the King James reads as the house of David; readers differ on which house is meant.
In Jewish prayer books it's said each morning, and at Hanukkah, the feast of the temple's rededication. Some churches read it in the Easter season.
The psalm doesn't say the night isn't real.

teach.h: WEEPING MAY ENDURE FOR A NIGHT.
teach.b: It says the night isn't permanent.

how: Some churches read Psalm 30 in the Easter season, Christians pray it in times of recovery and thanksgiving, and its line 'joy cometh in the morning' is said at funerals and bedsides.

he gave all his money away.
games.why: "In my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved." then trouble came, he cried out, and God turned his mourning into dancing.

practice: Find whatever light there is, morning sun, a lamp, a window, and notice where it falls and what color it is. Think of one night in your life that felt endless, and that ended; you got through it.
If you're in a long night now, you don't have to feel joy yet, just remember that mornings come, and if you pray, give thanks for one morning.
